```{r }
#| label: Data Preparation

clusterfiles <- unlist(strsplit(params$clusterList, ","))
histofiles <- unlist(strsplit(params$histoList, ","))
tablefiles <- unlist(strsplit(params$tableList, ","))

```

# Introduction

In this analysis, we aim to generate the total number of different nanobody CDR3s that exist in a library, and the relative abundance of each. For our initial analysis we follow some of the steps used by Deschaght et al (2017).

# Results

In the first section, we briefly summarise the characteristics of the clusters. In the second one, we look more in detail at the CDR3 in the libraries.

## Clusters

In the following, we review the distribution of members of clusters and their sequence identity to the representative. The first plot shows, for every cluster size (x), how many clusters have that size (y), on logarithmic axes so that every cluster is drawn, from the singletons to the largest clones.

```{r}
#| label: ClusterMembership

# Legge i dati di cluster da ciascun file nella lista e li combina in un unico dataframe.

clusterbig <- data.frame()
for (file in clusterfiles) {
    samplename <- gsub("_clusters.summary", "", file)
    clusterdata <- read_csv(file)
    clusterdata$Sample <- samplename
    clusterbig <- rbind(clusterbig, clusterdata)
    rm(clusterdata)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: ClusterSizePlot

# Distribuzione delle dimensioni dei cluster: per ogni dimensione, quanti cluster la hanno.
# Assi logaritmici e nessun limite, così compaiono tutti i cluster, dai singoletti ai più grandi.
# dplyr::count perché seqinr, caricato dopo, ha una funzione count diversa.

clusterbig %>%
    dplyr::count(Sample, Count, name = "Clusters") %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = Count, y = Clusters)) +
    geom_point(size = 1) +
    scale_x_log10(breaks = scales::breaks_log(n = 7), labels = scales::label_comma()) +
    scale_y_log10(breaks = scales::breaks_log(n = 7), labels = scales::label_comma()) +
    xlab("Number of Cluster Members (log scale)") +
    ylab("Number of Clusters (log scale)") +
    ggtitle("Cluster Sizes") +
    facet_wrap(~Sample)
```

```{r}
#| label: clusterMembersPlot

# Genera un grafico a dispersione che mostra l'identità della sequenza rispetto al rappresentante del cluster.
# I cluster singleton hanno Identity = NA (nessun membro da confrontare) e vengono esclusi.

ggplot(data = clusterbig %>% filter(!is.na(Identity))) +
    geom_point(aes(x = Count, y = Identity), position = "jitter") +
    xlab("Number of Cluster Members") +
    ylab("Mean Sequence Identity of Members\nto Cluster Representative (%)") +
    facet_wrap(~Sample)
```

We summarise cluster counts based on the number of member sequences.

```{r}
#| label: clustercountsTable

# Crea una tabella che riassume il numero di cluster in base alla dimensione del cluster.
# Total_sequences e' il denominatore necessario per calcolare le frazioni clonali
# (quota della libreria occupata dal clone dominante e dai primi dieci cloni).

clusterbig$five <- clusterbig$Count >= 5
clusterbig$hundred <- clusterbig$Count >= 100
clusterbig$thousand <- clusterbig$Count >= 1000

clustercounts <- clusterbig %>%
    group_by(Sample) %>%
    summarize(
        Clusters = n(),
        Clusters_of_5 = sum(five),
        Clusters_of_100 = sum(hundred),
        Clusters_of_1000 = sum(thousand),
        Total_sequences = sum(Count),
        Top1_count = max(Count),
        Top10_count = sum(sort(Count, decreasing = TRUE)[1:min(10, n())])
    )

kable(clustercounts) %>%
    kable_styling()
```

## CDR3 analysis

The CDR3 of each cluster is annotated with nanoCDR-X (Bagordo et al. 2026) on the most frequent sequence of the cluster, not on the representative chosen by CD-HIT, which is the longest member and in large clusters is often an atypical sequence. The reference definition is CDR3-IMGT, positions 105–117 of the IMGT unique numbering, between the conserved cysteine 104 and tryptophan 118, both excluded (Lefranc et al. 2003); the agreement of the nanoCDR-X calls with it is reported in the CDR3 annotation QC of the interactive report. We also compute the length distribution of these CDR3 sequences.

```{r }
#| label: cdrhistogram

# Legge i dati degli istogrammi CDR3 da ciascun file e li combina in un unico dataframe.

cdrhists <- data.frame()
for (file in histofiles) {
    samplename <- gsub("_cdr3.hist", "", file)
    histdata <- read.csv(file, header = TRUE)
    colnames(histdata)[1:2] <- c("Size", "Count")
    histdata$Sample <- rep(samplename, times = nrow(histdata))
    cdrhists <- rbind(cdrhists, histdata)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: CDR3countsTable

# Crea una tabella che riassume il numero di CDR3 unici per campione.

cdrcounts <- cdrhists %>%
    group_by(Sample) %>%
    summarize(Unique_CDR3s = sum(Count))

kable(cdrcounts) %>%
    kable_styling()
```

```{r}
#| label: CDR3sizeplot

# Genera un istogramma della distribuzione delle dimensioni delle sequenze CDR3 uniche.

ggplot(data = cdrhists) +
    geom_histogram(aes(x = Size, y = Count), stat = "identity") +
    facet_wrap(~Sample) +
    ggtitle("Size Distribution of Unique CDR3s")
```

## Evolution of CDR3

Every cluster is joined to its CDR3 and to the metadata of its sample (individual, immunisation, boost), and the result is written to `cdr3_boost_overview_table.tsv`. When the pipeline is run with `--calculate_tree`, the CDR3s of the clusters with more than `cluster_size_threshold` members are aligned with ClustalOmega for each individual, and a neighbour-joining tree is drawn below.

```{r }
#| label: fastaRep

# Legge i dati delle sequenze fasta da ciascun file e li combina in un unico dataframe.

fastaSeq <- data.frame()
for (fasta in tablefiles) {
    sample <- gsub("_cdr3.tsv", "", fasta)
    seqs <- read_tsv(fasta)
    fastaSeq <- rbind(
        fastaSeq,
        cbind(seqs,
            sample = sample
        )
    )
    rm(seqs)
}
```

```{r}
#| label:  mergeData

# Unisce i dati dei cluster con i dati delle sequenze fasta.

boostEvol <- clusterbig
    clusterbig$Representative <- as.character(clusterbig$Representative)
    fastaSeq$ID <- as.character(fastaSeq$ID)

boostEvol <- clusterbig %>%
    left_join(fastaSeq,
        by = c(
            "Representative" = "ID",
            "Sample" = "sample"
        )
    )
```

```{r}
#| label: sampleMetaData

# Unisce i dati risultanti con i metadati del campione e salva il risultato in un file TSV.

boostEvol <- boostEvol %>%
    left_join(sampleMetaData,
        by = c("Sample" = "ID")
    )
write_tsv(boostEvol, "cdr3_boost_overview_table.tsv")
```

```{r eval=dotree}
#| label: MSAandTreeStore

# Questa sezione esegue l'allineamento multiplo delle sequenze CDR3 e genera un albero filogenetico per ciascun individuo.

individualData <- list()
treeDataList <- list()
treeMetaDataList <- list()
treePlotList <- list()

for (ind in unique(boostEvol$individual)) {
    tmpData <- boostEvol %>%
        filter(individual == ind) %>%
        filter(!is.na(CDR3)) %>%
        filter(Count > sizeThreshold) %>%
        group_by(CDR3) %>%
        summarise(
            clusterSize = max(Count),
            representativeSeq = Representative[which(Count == max(Count))],
            individual = individual[which(Count == max(Count))],
            sample = Sample[which(Count == max(Count))],
            immunisation = immunisation[which(Count == max(Count))],
            boost = boost[which(Count == max(Count))]
        ) %>%
        mutate(
            tip_label = paste0(
                representativeSeq, "_S", individual, "_I", immunisation, "_B", boost
            )
        )

    individualData[[ind]] <- tmpData

    individualCDR3 <- AAStringSet(tmpData$CDR3)
    names(individualCDR3) <- tmpData$tip_label

    if (length(individualCDR3) == 0) {
        message(paste("No CDR3 sequences found for individual", ind))
        next
    }

    if (!requireNamespace("msa", quietly = TRUE)) {
        message(paste("Package 'msa' is not installed. Skipping alignment and tree generation for individual", ind))
        next
    }

    # message("---> multiple alignment")
    msa <- msa::msa(individualCDR3, method = "ClustalOmega", type = "protein")
    alignment <- msa::msaConvert(msa, type = "seqinr::alignment")

    # message("---> tree generation")
    dist <- dist.alignment(alignment)
    smalltree <- njs(dist) # to allow for missing values in the distance matrix

    # message("---> tree metadata")
    treeMetaData <- tmpData[c("tip_label", "sample", "individual", "immunisation", "boost")]

    # message("---> store results")
    treeDataList[[ind]] <- smalltree
    treeMetaDataList[[ind]] <- treeMetaData

    # message("---> combine metadata in plot")
    treePlotBase <- ggtree(smalltree, layout = "rectangular") %<+% treeMetaData

    # message("---> generate tree plot")
    annotatedTree <- treePlotBase +
        geom_tiplab(align = TRUE, linesize = .2, size = 2, offset = -0.8) +
        geom_rootpoint(color = "black", size = 3) +
        geom_tippoint(aes(color = boost), size = 2, alpha = .5)

    treePlotList[[ind]] <- annotatedTree
}

```

```{r}
#| label: setOut
out <- NULL
```

```{r eval=dotree}
#| label: run-summary-md
#| include: false

# Esegue il rendering dei documenti figlio per ciascun individuo, utilizzando i dati dell'evoluzione delle sequenze CDR3.

out <- NULL
for (ind in unique(boostEvol$individual)) {
    env <- new.env()
    out <- c(out, knit_child(loopFile, envir = env))
}

```

# Methods

The overall approach is inspired by the work *Large diversity of Functional Nanobodies from a Camelid Immune Library Revealed by an Alternative Analysis of Next-Generation sequencing data* by Pieter Deschaght and colleagues (doi: 10.3389/fimmu.2017.00420, published April 2017).

## Merging forward and reverse reads

Forward and reverse reads are merged with FLASH (Magoč and Salzberg 2011) with its default settings (minimum overlap 10 bp, maximum expected overlap 65 bp, maximum mismatch density 0.25) and one thread (`-t 1`), so that the merged reads are written in the order of the input reads and the clusters are the same in every run. More information about the software is available at their [website](https://ccb.jhu.edu/software/FLASH/)

## Translating cDNA to protein sequence

The VHH region of each merged read is translated with an in-house Python script based on Biopython. The region starts at the first DNA encoding of one of the start motifs *MAQ*, *QVQ*, *EVQ*, *VQL* or *LQL*, and ends with the motif *TVSS*: the first *TVSS* in frame that starts 7 residues after the tryptophan of the framework-4 motif *WG.G*, its position in the IMGT germline, or the first *TVSS* of the read when none is in that position. When the start or the end motif is missing on the forward strand, the reverse complement is searched. Reads in which no exact motif is found on either strand are searched again in the six reading frames with anchors that tolerate one amino-acid substitution, confirmed by residues conserved in the IMGT germline of the alpaca (the framework-1 cysteine, the second cysteine and the *WG.G* motif). A region that is not a multiple of three nucleotides, or whose translation contains a stop codon or an undetermined residue (X) or is shorter than 70 residues, is discarded: a complete VHH is longer than 100 residues, and shorter translations are primer dimers or fragments of the VHH. The translation log counts the reads in each of these cases, and the sequence accounting table of the interactive report shows them for every sample.

## Clustering the aminoacid sequences

Clustering of the translated sequences is performed using the software CD-HIT (Li and Godzik 2006). For more information, please visit their [website](https://github.com/weizhongli/cdhit/wiki). This run used an identity threshold of `r params$cdhitIdentity` (parameter `cdhit_identity`; the default, 0.9, is the threshold of Deschaght et al.) and a word size of `r params$cdhitWordSize`, with global identity. Each sequence joins the cluster of its most similar representative (`-g 1`), and identity ties go to the cluster created first (`-det 1`, from the reproducible build of CD-HIT 4.8.1 in [lescailab/cdhit](https://github.com/lescailab/cdhit/tree/reproducible)), so that the clusters do not depend on the number of threads or on the memory available.

## Extracting the CDR3 sequences

The CDR3 is annotated with nanoCDR-X (Bagordo et al. 2026), a deep-learning model for nanobody CDR annotation, on one sequence per cluster: its most frequent sequence. CD-HIT makes the longest sequence of a cluster its representative, and in large clusters the longest sequence is often an atypical one, for example with an extra stretch after framework 4, on which the CDR3 is read wrongly or not at all. The reference definition of the CDR3 is CDR3-IMGT (Lefranc et al. 2003): the residues between the second conserved cysteine (IMGT position 104) and the J-region tryptophan (IMGT position 118), both excluded, which is also the `cdr3` field of the AIRR Community standard (Vander Heiden et al. 2018). The interactive report compares every nanoCDR-X call with this definition, locating the two anchors with sequence motifs.
